extracted.intended_audience: postsecondary institutions (Title IX coordinators, investigators, decision-makers), institutional administrators, and legal counsel responsible for Title IX grievance processes
extracted.subtask_description: Regulatory guidance and standards for how recipients (postsecondary institutions) must respond to reports and formal complaints of sexual harassment, including procedural safeguards, training, evidence rules, standards of proof, and remedies. Focused on implementing §106.44/§106.45 obligations under Title IX.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presumption of Non-Responsibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 106.45(b)(1)(iv) — a presumption that the respondent is not responsible throughout the grievance process; the presumption helps ensure proper application of the selected standard of evidence and that recipients do not treat the respondent as responsible until proved responsible (subject to enumerated exceptions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presumption's purpose includes reinforcing that the burden of proof remains on the recipient (not on the respondent). The presumption does not permit recipients to apply a criminal 'beyond a reasonable doubt' standard; its operation is particularly important where a recipient selects the preponderance of the evidence standard so that in cases where evidence is in equipoise (50/50) the result is non-responsibility. See also discussion in the 'Section 106.45(b)(7)(i) Standard of Evidence' subsection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supportive Measures for Complainants
rubrics_metrics.description: Recipients must treat complainants equitably by offering supportive measures (see §106.44(a)), which preserve equal educational access and assist complainants after alleged sexual harassment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supportive measures must not 'unreasonably burden' the other party (§106.30). Recipients may continue to provide supportive measures regardless of case outcome. Recipients must engage in an interactive discussion with the complainant to arrive at helpful measures and may document reasons regarding response and deliberate indifference under §106.45(b)(10).

rubrics_metrics.name: Live Hearing and Cross-Examination Requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 106.45(b)(6)(i) — either party has the right to a live hearing and cross-examination (which may occur in separate rooms); cross-examination must be conducted by the party's advisor, not the party directly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The decision-maker must not rely on the statement of a party or witness who does not submit to cross-examination, resulting in exclusion of untested statements. Institutions may provide advisors to conduct cross-examination; advisors need not be unbiased or conflict-free and recipients have latitude on training for such advisors because the advisor's role is to conduct cross-examination on behalf of a party.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rape Shield Protections (Limits on Prior Sexual Behavior/Predisposition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 106.45(b)(6) — questions and evidence about a complainant's sexual predisposition or prior sexual behavior are not relevant except: (1) to prove someone other than the respondent committed the conduct alleged, or (2) specific incidents of prior sexual behavior between the complainant and respondent offered to prove consent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This provision is explicitly designed to protect complainants from invasive inquiries; the hearing rule allowing separate rooms and the rape-shield rule operate as complainant-specific protections within the grievance process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relevance of Evidence and Investigative Report Requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Final regulations do not define 'relevance' — ordinary meaning applies. Only 'relevant' evidence may be subject to decision-maker's objective evaluation. Determinations about relevance are made when finalizing the investigative report, which must 'fairly summarize all relevant evidence' (§106.45(b)(5)(vii)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The universe of evidence given to parties for inspection and review must consist of all evidence directly related to the allegations (§106.45(b)(5)(vi)). Recipients may adopt rules or train decision-makers about assigning weight to types of relevant evidence so long as such rules apply equally to both parties and respect rape-shield and privilege exceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Privilege Exception for Evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 106.45(b)(1)(x) — a recipient may not use information or evidence protected by a legally recognized privilege unless the privilege holder has waived it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Privileged information is not available for use in the grievance process absent a waiver; this operates as an exception to what evidence can be considered even if otherwise 'relevant.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Impartiality and Conflict-of-Interest Prohibition
rubrics_metrics.description: The grievance process must be conducted impartially and free from conflicts of interest or bias for or against complainants or respondents; self-selected rules must apply equally to both parties (§106.45(b) and related provisions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A recipient's manner of adopting or applying evaluation rules could itself be sex discrimination. Decision-makers must be different from any individual serving as a Title IX Coordinator or investigator (§106.45(b)(7)(i)), though Title IX Coordinators may serve as investigators; the final regulations do not prescribe per se administrative-reporting-chain restrictions as automatic conflicts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Training Requirements for Title IX Personnel
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 106.45(b)(1)(iii) — Title IX personnel (coordinators, investigators, decision-makers, and facilitators of informal resolution) must receive training on their roles, including trauma-informed practices, evaluating evidence, conducting investigations, and the scope of the institution's education program or activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Training now includes conducting appeals and scope of the program or activity. The preamble references 2014 Q&A recommended topics (working with victims, sexual violence conduct types, preponderance standard, consent, role of drugs/alcohol, credibility, evidence evaluation, confidentiality, trauma effects, cultural awareness). Traumatic-memory considerations warrant balanced approaches: trauma-informed training should avoid sex stereotypes and should not cause adjudicators to overlook noteworthy inconsistencies that bear on due process.

rubrics_metrics.name: No Training/Conflict Requirement for Advisors Provided by Recipient
rubrics_metrics.description: Final regulations impose no prohibition on conflicts of interest or bias for advisors the recipient provides to a party, nor any training requirement for such advisors, to preserve recipient flexibility in complying with the requirement to provide an advisor for cross-examination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department reasons advisors need not be unbiased because their role is to conduct cross-examination on behalf of a party; recipients may choose to provide training or set qualifications but are not required to do so.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeals Requirement and Training on Appeals
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 106.45(b)(8) requires recipients to offer appeals; §106.45(b)(1)(iii) training has been revised to include conducting appeals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appeals are a mandatory procedural component; institutions must ensure personnel who handle appeals are appropriately trained.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection and Uniform Application of Standard of Evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 106.45(b)(1)(vii) — recipients must select and apply the same standard of evidence (either preponderance of the evidence or clear and convincing evidence) to all Title IX sexual harassment cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department notes the preponderance standard is the lowest permissible; where preponderance is selected, the presumption of non-responsibility helps ensure non-responsibility when evidence is in equipoise. See related discussion in §106.45(b)(7)(i).

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of Proof Allocation — Burden on the Recipient
rubrics_metrics.description: Final regulations allocate the burden of proof on the recipient (not on complainant or respondent) to prove that the respondent committed sexual harassment (§106.45(b)(1)(i); §106.45(b)(7)(iv)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts have indicated allocating the burden to the recipient, together with other procedural safeguards, is constitutionally permissible. The presumption of non-responsibility reinforces that the burden remains on the recipient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Documentation that Response Was Not Deliberately Indifferent
rubrics_metrics.description: Recipients must document their reasons for concluding that their response to sexual harassment was not deliberately indifferent (referenced to §106.45(b)(10) in the preamble).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Documentation supports determinations about adequacy of institutional responses and is part of compliance recordkeeping.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emergency Removal and Administrative Leave Exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Sections §106.44(c) and §106.44(d) — recipients may take certain adverse actions (e.g., emergency removal of a student or administrative leave for an employee) prior to the conclusion of a grievance process if the respondent poses an immediate threat to physical health or safety.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such removals are exceptions to the general rule forbidding adverse treatment before a grievance process conclusion; recipients must provide a post-removal opportunity to challenge the removal where required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Facilitation of Informal Resolution Processes
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 106.45(b)(9) — a recipient may facilitate an informal resolution process (except for allegations that an employee sexually harassed a student); informal resolution may result in parties and the recipient agreeing to a resolution that involves disciplining a respondent, with informed, written, voluntary consent of both parties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Informal resolution, when properly consented to, complies with requirement that recipients not discipline respondents without following a grievance process that complies with §106.45 because §106.45 itself authorizes informal resolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusion of Untested Statements in Decision-Making
rubrics_metrics.description: Because §106.45(b)(6)(i) requires live hearings and cross-examination, the decision-maker must not rely on statements of parties or witnesses who do not submit to cross-examination, effectively excluding untested statements from consideration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This approach limits hearsay-like reliance in adjudication of formal complaints; the preamble notes this results in exclusion of statements that remain untested by cross-examination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equal Application of Evidentiary Rules and Weighting
rubrics_metrics.description: Recipients may adopt rules or provide training regarding how to assign weight to a given type of relevant evidence, provided such rules apply equally to both parties and respect rape-shield and privilege exceptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While recipients can guide decision-makers on weighting evidence types, such guidance cannot create unequal treatment or constitute sex discrimination in how evidence is evaluated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on Retaliation and Handling of False Statements
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 106.71 prohibits retaliation; paragraph (b)(2) cautions that a determination regarding responsibility alone is not sufficient to conclude a party made a materially false statement in bad faith. Recipients retain discretion to address false statements under their own codes of conduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutions must avoid retaliatory actions and cannot automatically treat an adverse finding as proof of a materially false statement for disciplinary purposes without separate findings; handling of false statements may be governed by institutional codes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provision and Scope of Evidence Disclosure to Parties
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 106.45(b)(5)(vi) — the universe of evidence given to the parties for inspection and review must consist of all evidence directly related to the allegations; investigative reports must fairly summarize all relevant evidence (§106.45(b)(5)(vii)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Full disclosure of directly related evidence is required for inspection and review; relevancy determinations are made when finalizing the investigative report and only relevant evidence is subject to the decision-maker's objective evaluation, subject to rape-shield and privilege exceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of Complainants' Unique Needs in Process Design
rubrics_metrics.description: The grievance process contains provisions responsive to the unique needs of complainants (e.g., rape shield protections; separate-room live hearings) and requires treating complainants as victims in need of services under §106.44(a) even before fact-finding is concluded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These protections aim to preserve complainants' access to education and limit retraumatization; the preamble explains these are not unfair to respondents because parallel procedural rights apply to both parties and exceptions for emergency safety exist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Training and Practices Should Avoid Sex Stereotypes and Bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Training programs (including trauma-informed training) should be 'fair, equitable, nuanced' and must not 'rely on sex stereotypes' or otherwise introduce impermissible bias into investigations and adjudication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department cites scholarship recommending diversity/implicit-bias training but warns that trauma-informed approaches to evaluating evidence must be grounded in current science and balanced so adjudicators do not ignore noteworthy inconsistencies relevant to due process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flexibility to Provide Legal Representation to Address Disparities
rubrics_metrics.description: Recipients are not required to provide legal representation to parties but may choose to offer both parties legal representation to address disparities in financial ability to hire counsel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department recognizes only a fraction of postsecondary institutions provide legal representation to both parties, but maintains institutions may do so to address equity concerns.
